separation_content_v2: Controllers keep aircraft separated to prevent collisions and wake encounters. This classroom model uses 3 nautical miles horizontally or 1,000 feet vertically; it expands horizontal spacing to 6 nautical miles for a pair involving a heavy or super aircraft. Real separation rules depend on airspace, equipment, flight phase, and the leading and following aircraft. Wake vortices can remain hazardous after the aircraft passes, so extra spacing and flight-path awareness matter.
separation_formula_v2: Model conflict: horizontal spacing below 3nm (6nm with heavy/super) AND vertical spacing below 1,000ft
sequencing_content_v2: Sequencing means choosing a landing order and spacing aircraft so the runway is ready for each arrival. Distance alone does not determine who arrives first: a faster aircraft farther away may catch a slower one. Compare their estimated arrival times, then consider wake category, runway assignment, and emergency priority. These estimates assume constant groundspeed along the remaining route; vectors, holding, and speed changes alter them.
sequencing_formula_v2: ETA in minutes = remaining route distance in nm / groundspeed in knots × 60
vectors_content_v2: Controllers issue heading instructions, called vectors, to guide aircraft toward a route or approach. Headings run clockwise from north: 090° is east, 180° is south, and 270° is west. At a standard turn rate of 3° per second, a full circle takes two minutes, but aircraft do not always use that rate. At the same bank angle, higher airspeed produces a larger turn radius. Wind can make the ground track differ from the heading.
vectors_formula_v2: Level-turn radius = airspeed² / (g × tan(bank)); use m/s for airspeed and 9.81 m/s² for g to get meters
communication_content_v2: Standard phrases help pilots and controllers understand each other. An approach clearance permits the approach; a landing clearance permits landing on the assigned runway. A go-around stops the landing attempt and begins a climb. Pilots acknowledge instructions and read back key details such as runway, heading, and altitude so errors can be caught. Roger means the message was received, while Wilco means it was understood and will be followed. The phonetic alphabet begins Alfa, Bravo, Charlie.
communication_formula_v2: Read back key details: callsign + runway / heading / altitude + clearance
weather_content_v2: Thunderstorms, poor visibility, and strong winds can reduce runway capacity or change routes. Aircraft generally take off and land into the wind when practical, while runway selection also depends on traffic, runway condition, and procedures. Wind directions describe where the wind comes from. Split wind into a headwind or tailwind component along the runway and a crosswind component across it. An acceptable crosswind depends on the specific aircraft flight manual and operating conditions; there is no single limit for every aircraft.
weather_formula_v2: Headwind = wind speed × cos(angle); crosswind magnitude = |wind speed × sin(angle)|. Negative headwind means tailwind.

separation_content: Controllers must maintain minimum separation between aircraft: 3 nautical miles horizontally OR 1,000 feet vertically. For heavy aircraft (wake turbulence), 6nm is required behind. A 747 creates wingtip vortices that can flip a small plane — these invisible tornadoes persist for up to 3 minutes.
sequencing_content: Sequencing is the core skill of ATC: deciding the order aircraft land. Factors include: distance from airport, speed, aircraft type (heavies need more spacing), runway assignment, and fuel state (emergency = priority). A good controller builds a smooth, evenly-spaced line of aircraft — like merging highway traffic, but in 3D.
vectors_content: Controllers issue heading instructions ("vectors") to guide aircraft. A 360° turn takes about 2 minutes at standard rate (3°/second). To intercept a course, the vector must account for the turn radius. Wide-body jets have larger turn radii than small planes — like the difference between a bus and a bicycle turning a corner.
communication_content: Aviation uses standardized phrases to prevent misunderstanding. "Cleared to land" is permission to touch down. "Go around" means abort the landing and climb. Every instruction gets a "readback" — the pilot repeats it so the controller can verify. The phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie...) prevents letter confusion over radio.
weather_content: Weather is the #1 factor in ATC delays. Thunderstorms force route changes. Low visibility reduces runway capacity (aircraft need more spacing for instrument approaches). Wind direction determines which runway to use — aircraft always land INTO the wind when possible. A 15kt crosswind is challenging; 25kt is the limit for many aircraft.
